Vulnerability is the proneness of an individual or group to harm, exploitation or deprivation arising from external social, economic or structural forces. It is not a personal failing but a condition produced by society.

notes: Group nature: vulnerability is collective and not individual.
Structural roots: embedded in caste hierarchies, patriarchy and economic inequality.
Multidimensional impact: social, economic, political, physical and psychological domains.
Self-reinforcing cycle: poverty leads to poor health and education, which in turn deepens poverty.
The Government of India Act, 1935 classified disadvantaged groups into Scheduled Castes, Scheduled Tribes and Other Backward Classes.
Over the years the list has expanded to include women, children, the elderly, persons with disabilities, sexual minorities, denotified tribes and religious minorities.
The Ministry of Social Justice and Empowerment is the nodal ministry for the empowerment of these groups.

notes.h: Concept OF Social Justice AND Social Empowerment

body: Social justice means fair distribution of resources, opportunities and dignity across all sections of society. It seeks to correct historical wrongs and create substantive equality, not merely formal equality before law.

notes.h: Constitutional vision of social justice (three layers)

notes: Preamble: secures justice (social, economic and political), equality of status and dignity for all citizens.

Fundamental Rights: Article 14 (equality before law), Article 15 (prohibition of discrimination), Article 17 (abolition of untouchability), Article 21 (right to life with dignity) and Article 23 (prohibition of forced labour).
Directive Principles: Articles 38, 39, 41, 46 and 47, which guide the State towards becoming a welfare State.

body: Number card: FR articles 14, 15, 17, 21, 23 · DPSP articles 38, 39, 41, 46, 47.

Social empowerment is the practical expression of this vision. It means helping disadvantaged groups gain control over their lives through education, economic opportunity, political voice and barrier-free participation as equal citizens.

notes.h: Inclusive Growth, Income Inequality AND Social Justice

notes: Economic growth without inclusion deepens inequality and weakens social justice. India has shown high growth but still has poor human development indicators, which makes the inclusive growth agenda central to social justice.
India's top 10% holds more than 57% of national income while the bottom 50% holds around 13% (World Inequality Report 2022).
Inclusive growth widens demand, builds human capital and reduces social tensions.
It requires investment in health, education, skill development and social safety nets.

body: The relationship between growth and justice is mutual: growth provides resources for welfare, while welfare ensures growth reaches everyone.

Social infrastructure is the network of public services and institutions that enable human development. It includes schools, hospitals, anganwadis, sanitation facilities, drinking water systems, social security networks and public housing.

notes: India spends only 1.8% of GDP on public health against the recommended 2.5% (Economic Survey 2025-26).
Combined Centre and State spending on education is around 4.6% of GDP, below the 6% target of NEP 2020.
Wide interstate variations remain, with Kerala and Tamil Nadu doing far better than Bihar, UP and Jharkhand.

body: Strong social infrastructure is the precondition for any welfare scheme to succeed. Without good schools, functioning health centres and accessible institutions even the best-designed schemes fail at the last mile.

notes.h: Conceptual AND Philosophical Basis OF Welfare Schemes

body: Welfare schemes flow from the idea of a welfare State where the government takes responsibility for the well-being of its citizens, especially those who cannot protect themselves through the market.

notes: Article 38: State shall promote welfare of the people.
Article 39: equitable distribution of resources.
Article 46: special care of weaker sections.
Article 47: raising the standard of living and public health.
Reduction of poverty and inequality: MGNREGA provided employment to over 11 crore rural households.
Building human capital: PM-JAY offers health insurance to over 55 crore beneficiaries.
Provision of public goods: Samagra Shiksha expands school education.
Crisis resilience: PMGKAY and MGNREGA cushioned the poor during the COVID-19 pandemic.
Promoting equity: gives the disadvantaged a fair starting line.

notes.h: Discriminatory Nature Debate OF Welfare Design PYQ 2023

body: PYQ 2023 (15 marks): Development and welfare schemes for the vulnerable, by its nature, are discriminatory in approach. Do you agree? Give reasons for your answer.

head: Arguments that welfare schemes are discriminatory
Arguments that they are not discriminatory but corrective
rows: They single out specific groups based on caste, gender or religion and may reinforce these identities rather than dissolve them.
The Constitution itself permits positive discrimination under Articles 15(4), 15(5) and 16(4) to remedy historical injustices.
General category groups in genuine economic distress are often excluded.
Equal treatment of unequals is itself unequal, as Aristotle and the Supreme Court have repeatedly held.
Scheme design can stigmatise beneficiaries, making them feel like permanent recipients of charity.
Welfare schemes try to create a level playing field rather than tilt it against anyone.
Targeted schemes may create dependency rather than self-reliance.
Indra Sawhney judgment (1992) upheld that affirmative action is a constitutional mandate, not discrimination.

body: The honest position: welfare schemes are differential by design but not discriminatory in intent. The challenge lies in ensuring they reach the most deprived within deprived groups, do not stigmatise beneficiaries and gradually build self-reliance.
Welfare delivery in India is a shared responsibility: the Centre designs and funds while the States implement on the ground. This sharing is both a strength and a source of friction.

Centrally Sponsored Schemes (CSS) are funded jointly by the Centre and States in agreed ratios. Major examples: MGNREGA, PM Awas Yojana, Samagra Shiksha, NHM, ICDS and POSHAN Abhiyaan.

notes: The B. K. Chaturvedi Committee (2011) and the NITI Aayog Sub-Group of Chief Ministers (2015) recommended rationalisation of CSS, to give States more flexibility, reduce overlaps and improve outcomes.
States can adapt schemes to local needs.
Reduced fragmentation makes delivery sharper.
States have skin in the game through cost sharing.
States complain of inadequate central funding when their share rises.
Vertical devolution by the 15th Finance Commission at 41% is welcome but States still depend heavily on tied transfers.
Differential capacity across States means rich States gain more flexibility than poor ones.
Centre often blames States for poor outcomes while not increasing untied funds.

body: Cooperative federalism through forums like the NITI Aayog Governing Council and the Inter-State Council is essential to bridge these tensions.
The biggest gap in Indian welfare is not in design but in delivery. India spends large sums on welfare yet outcomes lag because schemes fail at the last mile.

notes.h: ROLE OF Awareness AND Beneficiary Involvement PYQ 2019

body: PYQ 2019 (15 marks): Performance of welfare schemes that are implemented for vulnerable sections is not so effective due to absence of their awareness and active involvement at all stages of policy process. Discuss.

notes.h: Welfare performance suffers when beneficiaries are kept passive

notes: Awareness deficit: many genuine beneficiaries do not know which schemes apply to them.
Information asymmetry: lets middlemen exploit beneficiaries through fake fees and false promises.
Lack of voice in scheme design: programmes do not match real needs on the ground.
Weak grievance redressal: discourages people from reporting failures.
Low ownership: beneficiaries treat schemes as charity rather than rights.

body: Active involvement of communities through Gram Sabhas, Self Help Groups, ward sabhas and social audits transforms passive recipients into active stakeholders. MGNREGA social audits in Andhra Pradesh have shown how community involvement plugs leakages.

notes.h: Structural problems that block the last mile

notes: Inclusion and exclusion errors: India still has around 4.4 crore ghost ration cards even after Aadhaar seeding.
Leakages and corruption: a CAG report on Bihar PDS found 30 to 40% of foodgrains lost to leakage.
Bureaucratic apathy and frequent transfers of frontline staff.
Digital exclusion of the elderly, rural poor and those without smartphones.
Inter-state variations in administrative capacity.
Convergence failure between line departments.

body: Reforms such as Direct Benefit Transfer (DBT), JAM Trinity (Jan Dhan, Aadhaar, Mobile), One Nation One Ration Card and PM GatiShakti (for logistics) are improving delivery, but the human element of motivated frontline workers remains the weakest link.

notes.h: Welfare Schemes AND Social Exclusion PYQ 2014

body: PYQ 2014 (12.5 marks): Do government's schemes for up lifting vulnerable and backward communities by protecting required social resources for them, lead to their exclusion in establishing businesses in urban economies.

Welfare schemes are meant to include the excluded, but sometimes their design or implementation produces fresh exclusion. The 2014 question asked whether protective measures for vulnerable groups may end up excluding them from urban business opportunities.

notes: Protective ring effect: reservation in jobs and education builds a comfort zone but does not push beneficiaries into competitive entrepreneurship.
Urban informal economy is largely outside the protective scope of caste-based schemes.
Capital and network barriers keep SC, ST and OBC entrepreneurs out of mainstream business.
Stand Up India, the Venture Capital Fund for SCs and PM Vishwakarma are steps to close this gap, yet only a small fraction of MSME credit reaches Dalit and Tribal entrepreneurs.

body: The lesson: protection must be balanced with promotion. Reservation alone does not create an entrepreneurial class. It must be combined with credit access, market linkages, mentorship and skill upgradation.

PYQ 2021 (15 marks): Though women in post Independent India have excelled in various fields, the social attitude towards women and feminist movement has been patriarchial. Apart from women education and women empowerment schemes, what interventions can help change this milieu.

Patriarchy operates through silent codes that no law can directly touch. It shapes who eats first at home, who inherits land, who steps outside and who carries the family honour. Schemes can improve material conditions but attitudes need different tools.

notes: Engaging men and boys through programmes like HeForShe and the MARD initiative by Farhan Akhtar to shift masculinity norms.
Media and popular culture can break stereotypes through films, advertisements and digital content with positive women role models.
School curriculum reforms to integrate gender sensitivity, consent education and equal sharing of housework.
Religious and community leaders who can challenge patriarchal customs from within tradition.
Workplace cultural change through paternity leave, flexible hours and zero tolerance to harassment.
Legal reforms in personal laws and uniform inheritance rights to remove hidden discrimination.
Recognition of unpaid work in national income accounts to make women's contribution visible.

notes.h: WAY Ahead FOR Health IN India

body: India's health journey is at a turning point. NFHS 6 confirms historic gains in maternal and child health, immunisation, household insurance coverage and women's empowerment. India has made progress on MDGs and is on track for several SDG 3 targets. MMR has fallen by 86% since 1990 and TFR has stabilised below replacement level.

Yet the same data reveals a worrying transition: adult obesity, diabetes and hypertension are surging, especially in urban India; anaemia and exclusive breastfeeding show worrying trends; mental health remains a silent crisis; NCDs account for over 57% of all deaths.

notes: Investment: raise public health spending from 1.8% to the promised 2.5% of GDP.
Equity: close rural urban, gender, caste and tribal gaps in access.
Quality and accountability: enforce patient rights, regulate the private sector and protect healthcare workers.
Innovation: through ABDM, eSanjeevani, AI and AYUSH integration.

body: Four reforms, order free: Invest, Equalise, Quality-check, Innovate. Sentence: "Invest Early; Quality Improves." (own mnemonic)

notes: From a disease centric to a wellness centric model.
From urban tertiary care focus to grassroots primary care strength.
From market driven inequity to state led equity.

body: Health is not just a sector. It is the foundation of demographic dividend, economic growth and social justice. As Amartya Sen reminds us, the test of any society's progress is how it treats its most vulnerable. India's health system, with its strengths and gaps, is the most important measure of that test.
